sections.h2: What “AI exposure” means — and what it doesn’t
sections.html:
Every occupation on this site carries a score between zero and ten that measures its exposure to generative artificial intelligence. The score is built from the actual content of an occupation's day-to-day tasks: it asks how much of that task content generative AI can already perform, or meaningfully assist with, given the current capabilities of the technology. A ten would mean that almost every task sits within the reach of today's AI tools; a zero would mean there is essentially no overlap. Crucially, this is not a prediction about whether a job will exist in the future. Exposure is not the same as automation, and it is certainly not the same as job loss. Many occupations with high exposure will change dramatically, but the change may take the form of new ways of working rather than the removal of the role itself. The distinction matters because it shapes how we should think about policy, training and individual career decisions.

On the treemap, every occupation is shown as a rectangle. The area of each rectangle is proportional to the number of people working in that occupation, so a wide and tall tile represents a large share of the workforce. The colour of the tile encodes the exposure score, with green at the low end and red at the high end. A country with a large green tile is one where a substantial portion of the labour force sits in relatively low-exposure roles; a country with many red tiles is one where the workforce is more concentrated in tasks that AI can already handle. The scores themselves have been placed on a single global percentile scale, meaning that the same numerical score refers to the same position on the distribution everywhere. That is why the site can compare, for example, an occupation in Iceland with the equivalent occupation in India, even though the two labour markets are very different. The data cover forty-six countries, more than twenty-one thousand occupations and over two point three billion workers in total. Globally, the employment-weighted average exposure across all occupations is four point seven.

Looking at country-level averages gives a quick sense of how exposure varies. Iceland has the highest average at six point one, followed closely by Singapore and Luxembourg at six point zero, with Malaysia at five point nine and Switzerland and Germany at five point eight. At the other end, India has the lowest average at three point nine, with Thailand and Mexico at four point two and four point five respectively. These figures are not a league table of risk, because exposure is not a measure of vulnerability to job loss. Rather, they show how far the task structures of different economies currently overlap with the capabilities of generative AI. It is notable that the range across countries is relatively narrow compared with the range across occupations or industries. Most countries sit between roughly four and six, which suggests that the overall amount of task exposure is fairly similar, even if the mix of occupations differs.

The same pattern emerges when you look at industries. The global employment-weighted average exposure for Business, Finance and Legal is eight point one, and so too is the average for IT and Digital. Education and Community sits at five point nine, Engineering and Infrastructure at five point eight, and Government and Public Sector at five point seven. At the lower end, Healthcare and Care averages four point nine, Creative, Media and Personal Services four point six, Transport, Logistics and Mining four point three, Agriculture and Environment three point seven, and Trades and Construction just one point nine. These averages summarise a lot of variation within each industry, but they give a reliable sense of where the greatest overlap between existing tasks and current AI capabilities lies. The industries with the highest exposure are those that rely heavily on processing text, analysing data, drafting documents and generating content. The industries with the lowest exposure tend to involve physical manipulation, manual dexterity or direct interaction with people in ways that are harder to reproduce with a language model.

Repeating the central warning, none of these numbers tells you whether a particular person will lose their job. A high exposure score simply means that the tasks performed in an occupation are the kind that generative AI can already do or assist with. That is useful information because it tells you where the first point of change is likely to appear. But whether those tasks are actually automated, and at what speed, depends on many other factors: the cost of AI systems, the regulatory environment, the attitudes of employers, the willingness of workers to use new tools and the way that technology is embedded in existing workflows. In many cases, the likely outcome is that humans and AI work together, with the AI taking over some tasks and the human concentrating on the tasks that require judgement, creativity, emotional intelligence or complex decision making. Exposure is therefore best understood as a starting point for thinking about complementary skills, not as a prophecy about any individual's job.

Task exposure is a measure of how much the routine activities of an occupation overlap with the capabilities of generative AI, not a prediction of whether the job will disappear. Across the 46 countries and 21,049 occupations used in this analysis, the global employment-weighted average sits at 4.7 on a scale from zero to ten. That figure conceals a far more pronounced difference between industries than between countries. Business, Finance & Legal and IT & Digital both have an average exposure of 8.1, while Trades & Construction has an average of 1.9, a difference of 6.2 points. By comparison, country-level averages range only from Iceland at 6.1 to India at 3.9, a span of 2.2 points. This means that the nature of the sector, and the tasks that dominate it, matters more for exposure than the national labour market a worker happens to be in.

Industries that sit at the top are dominated by information work. Generative AI models are trained on text, code and structured data, so they are well suited to tasks such as writing and editing documents, translating between languages, answering questions, analyzing contracts, preparing financial statements, and generating or reviewing computer code. Business, Finance & Legal occupations and IT & Digital occupations both score 8.1 precisely because a large share of their day-to-day activities are symbolic rather than physical. A lawyer may spend hours reviewing prior judgments, a financial analyst may compare thousands of rows of accounts, and a software developer may write functions or explain code to colleagues; each of those activities involves producing or interpreting language or logic in a way that overlaps with what AI can do. That does not mean the human is removed, but the tasks themselves are open to substantial automation or augmentation.

The middle of the industry distribution shows that information work is not the only factor. Education & Community, with an average of 5.9, contains occupations that involve preparing materials, planning lessons, and assessing written answers, but also require managing a classroom, reading social cues, and offering personal encouragement. Engineering & Infrastructure, at 5.8, relies on drawings, calculations and project documentation, which are text-like and code-like, but also depends on site visits, physical inspection and installation work. Government & Public Sector, at 5.7, includes policy writing, casework and consultation responses, but also involves face-to-face public services and operational duties. These sectors therefore have a mixed exposure profile: a substantial amount of their work can be assisted by generative AI, but the human judgement and physical presence required in many roles pulls the average down from the 8.1 scored by the information-intensive sectors.

At the lower end, physical, manual and in-person work dominates. Healthcare & Care has an average of 4.9, which places it in the lowest-exposure list, but it is worth noting that this is the same numeric average as Hospitality, Retail & Tourism, which appears in the highest-exposure list. That apparent contradiction highlights the importance of looking inside broad sectors: a hospital has administrative workers who schedule appointments and write case notes, and their exposure may be high, but it also has nurses, care assistants and physiotherapists whose work involves lifting, moving, observing, and physically interacting with patients. Similarly, hospitality includes front-desk staff handling reservations and a large number of waiters, kitchen porters and housekeepers whose work cannot be reduced to text generation. Creative, Media & Personal Services, on 4.6, is a particularly mixed group: many creative production tasks involve editing text or images, but personal services such as hairdressing, beauty therapy or fitness training are firmly physical and interactive. Transport, Logistics & Mining, at 4.3, involves route planning and paperwork but also vehicle operation, loading and unloading, and extraction work in locations far from any screen. Agriculture & Environment, at 3.7, is weighted heavily toward weather-dependent, manual and outdoor tasks. Trades & Construction, at 1.9, is the clearest case: an electrician wiring a building, a carpenter measuring wood, or a scaffolder assembling a structure is carrying out tasks that require fine motor control, strength, and adaptation to unpredictable sites, almost none of which can be directly performed by a language model.

The comparison with country-level averages is instructive. For all 46 countries, the employment-weighted average ranges between 3.9 and 6.1, a spread of 2.2 points. For the broad industry groups in this dataset, the averages run from 1.9 to 8.1, a spread of 6.2 points. Seen this way, the type of work performed is considerably more influential than the country in which it is performed. That remains true even though the two are linked, because every country has a mixture of industries, and no country is composed entirely of high-exposure or low-exposure sectors. The wider point is that the character of the job, and the density of information tasks within it, is the central driver of generative AI exposure.

Ultimately, these exposure scores should be treated as a measure of how tasks are likely to change, not as a forecast of employment losses. An office-based role with a score of 8.1 may become more productive, with AI taking over drafting and summarising, but the human remains responsible for decisions and accountability. A construction role with a score of 1.9 is not immune to wider technological change, but the immediate impact of generative AI on the physical work itself is more limited. The central conclusion stands: across the 46 countries studied, the industry in which someone works tells you more about their exposure to generative AI than the country in which they live.

sections.h2: What high exposure means for workers — and the limits of the data
sections.html:
An occupation with a high exposure score does not mean a particular worker is marked for replacement, and still less does it mean the occupation itself is finished. It indicates that a substantial share of the tasks associated with that occupation, as described in official classifications, overlap with things generative AI tools can already do: handling structured information, producing and summarising text, translating between languages or formats, and generating credible first drafts. The score is a measure of task overlap, not a forecast of how quickly employers will adopt the technology or whether jobs will disappear. Even in occupations with the highest exposure, people are not just collections of routine tasks. A lawyer drafts contracts but also reassures a nervous client; an accountant prepares tax returns but also explains uncomfortable financial news to a small business owner; a software developer writes code but also discovers what the user actually needs. The practical response, therefore, is to look at your own weekly work and separate the components that are most likely to be automated or augmented from those that depend on human presence, judgement, empathy or responsibility. That working distinction, rather than the headline number, is what should guide your thinking about career development.

Generative AI is strongest when a task has a clear input and an output that a knowledgeable person can check. Drafting routine correspondence, summarising long documents, turning meeting notes into action lists, producing marketing copy, translating technical text, and writing basic code snippets are all areas where the technology acts as a useful assistant. The worker's role shifts towards framing the request, evaluating the result, correcting errors, and supplying context that the model lacks. By contrast, AI still struggles with tasks that require physical dexterity in unpredictable settings, genuine emotional connection in caring relationships, nuanced negotiation where the other party is reading you as much as you are reading them, and decisions that involve conflicting values, legal responsibility, or personal accountability. These are not marginal extras; they occur throughout many high-scoring occupations. Even a role dominated by writing or analysis includes moments when a client calls with an unusual worry or a manager asks for a judgement call in a new situation. Those moments will not dissolve just because the more routine elements have become easier.

The most useful skills in an AI-exposed occupation are therefore not the supposed opposite of AI, but the ability to work effectively alongside it. That means learning to give clear, specific instructions; breaking complex tasks into subtasks; and, above all, learning to check AI output critically. Language models are fluent but can be confidently wrong, so workers need enough domain knowledge to recognise a plausible error and enough verifiable habits to trace a claim back to its source. Data literacy, basic statistics, and structured evaluation are likely to become more valuable than remembering fixed procedures. At the same time, the capabilities that become relatively more important as routine tasks are automated are distinctly human ones: coordinating real people, interpreting ambiguous situations, building trust with clients and service users, exercising professional judgement, and taking responsibility for final decisions. These are not vague soft skills; they are the substance of professional work when a machine supplies a recommendation rather than a definitive answer. You can develop them by actively seeking roles or projects that involve direct contact, cross-functional collaboration, and accountability for outcomes, and by using AI tools to free time for that kind of work rather than treating them as a threat to be resisted.

The data themselves carry important limitations. Exposure scores are produced by mapping research indices about AI capabilities onto official occupation classifications, and in many cases that mapping is assisted by statistical models rather than hand-tuned for every occupation and country. This means every score comes with a margin of uncertainty. More fundamentally, the unit of analysis is the task, not the job. National classifications bundle many activities under a single occupation title, but two people with the same title can fill their days very differently. A chartered accountant in a large firm might spend hours extracting data from spreadsheets; a colleague in a small practice might spend almost the entire day speaking with clients. The exposure score describes the average full set of tasks in the classification, not your own time allocation. So before responding to an exposure figure for your occupation, draw up a rough list of your actual activities, note the share of time that goes to each, and ask which of them are routine and structured, which require reading a human situation, and which require you to stand behind the result. That personal exercise will usually tell you more than the occupation-level number.

Finally, the exposure data cannot forecast how quickly employers will introduce the technology, what choices they will make about redeploying staff, how many entirely new tasks and occupations will emerge, or how regulation and professional ethics will govern the tools. Adoption depends on far more than capability: the cost of integrating systems, concerns about confidentiality and liability, the willingness of managers to alter long-established routines, and the bargaining power of workers themselves. In some sectors the technology may be embedded cautiously as an optional assistant; in others it may be forced through rapidly as part of a new management system. A high exposure score could, in some cases, lead to fewer people doing the old tasks, but it could equally lead to the service becoming cheaper and demand expanding, or to workers spending their time on more complex parts of the job. History suggests that new technologies create categories of work that are hard to foresee from the categories of today. The exposure index is therefore best treated as a map of where task overlap currently exists, not as a prediction of who will gain or lose. Its purpose is to prompt questions, not to deliver a verdict on an individual's future.
